title: The tortoise draws in its limbs
hookLine: Arjuna asks how a person of steady wisdom sits, and Krishna answers with a tortoise
carry: pratyahara: senses drawn in like the tortoise
tomorrow: What does a steady eye see in everyone?

cards: The battlefield, before the fighting. Arjuna has just heard Krishna describe a person whose wisdom is steady, and he asks the most practical question in the whole Gita. In paraphrase: what does such a person look like?
How do they speak? How do they sit? How do they walk?
He doesn't want a theory. He wants to see it. And Krishna's answer begins with an animal nobody expects on a battlefield: a tortoise.

teach.h: THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.
teach.b: In chapter two, Krishna answers with a picture.

In paraphrase: when a person draws the senses back from the things of the senses, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs on every side, that person's wisdom is steady. A tortoise doesn't hate the world.
It just doesn't have to be pulled by every sound. It can draw in, and come out again. Yoga teachers often link this verse to pratyahara, Patanjali's word for drawing the senses in.
Then, in chapter six, Krishna answers the how-do-they-sit part almost literally. A clean place, a seat neither too high nor too low.

teach.h: HEAD AND NECK STILL, EYES LOWERED.
teach.b: In paraphrase: holding the body, head and neck straight and still, gazing at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking around in any direction.
The teacher Shankara reads it as if looking at the nose tip: eyes lowered and resting, not crossed. Trataka so far has needed a flame or an image out there. This gaze brings the point home.
And the very next verse says why.

teach.h: SIT WITH THE MIND ON ME.
teach.b: In paraphrase: calm, fearless, the mind held steady, let the yogi sit with the mind on me, intent on me. So the senses aren't drawn in to make an empty room. They're drawn in so the mind can rest on God.

That's the teaching: senses turned home, heart turned toward the Lord. Today the pull is a phone that lights up every few minutes, a feed built never to end. The Gita's answer isn't to hate the phone.
It's the tortoise: draw in, rest the mind on God, and come back out when you choose.

how: Many Hindus who meditate or sit for puja begin by drawing the senses in, eyes lowered and resting, following the Gita's picture of the tortoise and its instructions for sitting; yoga teachers call this drawing-in pratyahara.

s: in the Gita, the tortoise is a picture of running from the world
it's a picture of steadiness: the senses drawn in, and able to come out again.
the Gita's verse asks the meditator to cross the eyes at the nose
Shankara reads it as if looking at the nose tip: eyes lowered and resting, not crossed.
in chapter six, the senses are drawn in so the mind can rest on God
Krishna says to sit with the mind on him, intent on him.

games.q: you're Arjuna. you've asked Krishna how a person of steady wisdom lives. what picture does he give you?
o: a tortoise drawing in its limbs.
games.why: Krishna: the one who draws the senses back from their objects, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, is steady in wisdom.

practice: Sit upright, head and neck easy and straight, and let the eyes lower, half closed, resting as if looking toward the tip of the nose: no crossing, no strain, just no roaming.

Picture the tortoise drawing in its limbs, and let sounds and thoughts come and go without chasing them. If you pray, let the mind rest on a name of God you love; if not, rest it on the breath at the nostrils.
If the eyes ache, let them simply close.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today the point comes home: the senses drawn in like a tortoise's limbs, the eyes resting toward the tip of the nose.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: pratyahara, drawing back: the senses withdrawn from their objects. Patanjali's fifth limb of yoga.

carryVoice: Your line: pratyahara: senses drawn in like the tortoise. Draw in, then turn toward God. See you tomorrow.
